findings.source_quote: Each of these bears a significant dimension of the eternal God in their existence and gives us definition to their Creator.
findings.suggested_fix: Each of these bears a significant dimension of the eternal God in their existence and gives us definition to their Creator. (Translate the thought as: “Kila kimoja hudhihirisha katika uhai wake kipengele muhimu cha Mungu wa milele, na hutusaidia kumwelewa Muumba wake.”)
findings.translation_quote: Kila moja ya hivi hudhihirisha kwa namna ya pekee Mungu wa milele katika uhai wake na kutufundisha kuhusu Muumba wake.

findings.source_quote: The expression “happy as a lark” is so common a term that it is used by people who have never even ventured to the meadow to see or hear a lark.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a recognizable Kiswahili rendering or a brief target-language description for “lark” in both places, while retaining the comparison’s meaning; for example, “Usemi ‘mwenye furaha kama ndege wa mashambani’ ni wa kawaida sana ... kumwona au kumsikia ndege huyo.”
findings.translation_quote: Usemi “mwenye furaha kama ndege aina ya lark” ni wa kawaida sana hata hutumiwa na watu ambao hawajawahi kwenda shambani kumwona au kumsikia lark.

findings.source_quote: Wander near the nest of a swallow and you will find that they have ways of expressing depreciation as well.
findings.suggested_fix: Translate the bird name into Kiswahili (for example, “mbayuwayu”) and render “expressing depreciation” as expressing disapproval/displeasure, such as “Ukizunguka karibu na kiota cha mbayuwayu, utagundua kuwa nao wana njia za kuonyesha kutofurahishwa.”
findings.translation_quote: Ukitembea karibu na kiota cha mbayuwayu, utagundua kuwa nao wana njia za kuonyesha kutofurahishwa.

findings.source_quote: Some merely chirp with a merry heart.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace “hutweta” (pant) with a verb meaning chirp, such as “Baadhi yao hutoa milio midogo tu kwa moyo wa furaha.”
findings.translation_quote: Baadhi yao hutweta tu kwa moyo wa furaha.

findings.source_quote: The robin opens up the choir in early spring, but his song is soon surpassed in beauty by the song sparrow and again by the rose-breasted grosbeak. The song of the wren trumps them all for longevity and vibrancy.
findings.suggested_fix: Translate or describe the bird names in Kiswahili rather than leaving these common names in English; preserve the succession and comparisons, e.g. “ndege robin ... shomoro wa kuimba ... grosbeak mwenye kifua cha waridi ... ndege wren.”
findings.translation_quote: Robin huanzisha kwaya mwanzoni mwa masika, lakini wimbo wake hufunikwa upesi kwa uzuri na wimbo wa song sparrow, na baadaye tena na rose-breasted grosbeak. Wimbo wa wren unawazidi wote kwa urefu na uchangamfu.

findings.source_quote: Of such are the worthless blackbirds, starlings, and grackles.
findings.suggested_fix: Render the bird names in Kiswahili, or use concise Kiswahili descriptions if no conventional names are available, while preserving that the author identifies them as worthless examples.
findings.translation_quote: Miongoni mwao ni blackbirds, starlings, na grackles wasio na faida.

findings.source_quote: She will be found sitting on a high vantage, shamelessly calling to her lovers by her shrill screeching. She then has the audacity to lay her egg in another bird’s nest, forcing them to raise her offspring.
findings.suggested_fix: Translate “cowbird” with a Kiswahili description, e.g. “ndege cowbird,” consistently here; the description of its behavior is otherwise conveyed.
findings.translation_quote: Cowbird naye ni mweusi (jike ni wa kahawia/kijivu).

findings.source_quote: These are stopped-up wells like unto the wells that Isaac found upon his return to Gerar. The Philistines “had filled them with earth” (Gen 26:15).
findings.suggested_fix: Translate “stopped-up” as blocked or clogged, not “filled with earth” as a description of all the wells; preserve the following quoted wording and reference. For example: “Hivi ni visima vilivyozibwa, kama vile visima ambavyo Isaka alikuta aliporudi Gerari.”
findings.translation_quote: Hivi ni visima vilivyozibwa kwa udongo, kama vile visima ambavyo Isaka alikuta aliporudi Gerari.

findings.source_quote: … And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace” (Jer. 29:5-7).
findings.suggested_fix: Translate the full quoted excerpt faithfully, including the command to seek the city’s peace and the promise that its peace brings their peace; retain the reference numbers 29:5-7. For example: “... Itafutieni amani miji ambamo nimewapeleka mateka, na kuiombea kwa BWANA; kwa maana mkiwa na amani, ninyi pia mtakuwa na amani.”
findings.translation_quote: “… Naitafutieni amani miji ambayo nimewapeleka mateka, na kuiombea kwa BWANA; kwa maana katika amani yake ninyi mtakuwa na amani” (Yeremia 29:5-7).

findings.source_quote: If that isn’t enough, perhaps we should consider rising at early dawn and singing with the innumerable hosts of our feathered friends who are thankful for God’s loving providence.
findings.suggested_fix: Translate “feathered friends” as birds, rather than the more specific “friends with feathers,” e.g. “makundi yasiyohesabika ya ndege wanaomshukuru Mungu kwa majaliwa yake yenye upendo.”
findings.translation_quote: makundi yasiyohesabika ya marafiki zetu wenye manyoya wanaomshukuru Mungu kwa majaliwa yake yenye upendo
